newsitem.title: USA: IMF set to give a push to aid plan for world's poor.
newsitem.headline: IMF set to give a push to aid plan for world's poor.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund was set on Sunday to give its stamp of approval to an ambitious multi-billion dollar plan to provide debt relief to the world's poorest countries.

But the organization's policy-making Interim Committee was expected to leave open the thorny question of how the Fund will pay for its share of the program and whether it will need to sell off some of its gold to do so.
"I hope we will be able to have the first countries to benefit from (the debt initiative) ... before the end of the year," Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said.

Besides the debt plan, the IMF was also expected to discuss proposals to boost its resources for dealing with financial catastrophes and handling its day-by-day responsibilities as overseer of the world economy.
Also on the agenda: a suggestion by IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus that the Fund issue some $37 billion worth of its artificial currency to its member nations.
Sunday's meeting of the Interim Committee takes place against a background of an improving world economy.

"Conditions appear to be in place for a strengthening and broadening of the expansion of the world economy into 1997," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told reporters on Saturday after a six-hour meeting of the Group of Seven.

The G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- gave the multilateral debt relief initiative a big boost when it announced that creditor countries would sharply boost their assistance under the plan.
Rubin said the G7 and other creditor nations in the Paris Club are now prepared to write off up to 80 percent of their loans to eligible poor nations, up from 67 percent before.
These countries, many of them in Africa, have lost out in the burst of private money that is flooding into emerging economies, especially in Asia.
"Private investment is very selective, concentrated in only about 20 countries," Bangladesh Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria told reporters on Saturday.

Paris Club Chairman Christian Noyer said by telephone from France that there was no list of countries that will benefit first from the new terms of debt relief. But he said it was unlikely to be Uganda, cited by some World Bank officials as the first in line.
"Uganda, which has already benefited from a write-off of stock, is doing well," Noyer said. "It is not clear that it would be a priority."
The added Paris Club debt relief is supposed to dovetail with stepped-up assistance from the World Bank and the IMF and is designed to put poor nations back on their feet.
The World Bank has pledged to kick in $2 billion to the initiative. The IMF has also promised to do its part, but has not spelled out where it will find the money to participate.

The United States and Britain want the IMF to sell off up to five million ounces of its gold to aid the world's poor. But Italy, and especially Germany, are opposed and instead want the IMF to depend on direct donations from its members.
For now, they have decided to put off a decision on gold sales and launch the debt program with money the IMF already has in its kitty.
"We agreed to get going and leave the gold issue for resolution further down the road," Rubin said.
